title: Performance and Load Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of performance and load testing in MySQL and when it is useful.
Interpret or adapt the supplied sql example and predict its expected behavior.

content.intro: Learn performance and load testing in the context of testing and database quality. This lesson covers the supplied syllabus topic, demonstrates a representative MySQL example, and finishes with a verification task.
content.why_it_matters: An application connection is a trust boundary. Keep credentials outside source control, use parameterized queries for values, define transaction boundaries, and handle lost connections without assuming a request was never committed.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Capture an execution plan, record the starting query and result, change one index or query decision, and compare measurements. Write down the expected result before running the snippet. Compare actual output with the reference, then try one normal case and one edge case.

content_blocks.expected_output: The row is visible in the current transaction, then removed by ROLLBACK; use an isolated test schema.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a dedicated local MySQL lab using the stated MySQL release track. For schema-changing or administrative snippets, inspect every statement and use only a disposable schema; the in-page editor shows reference output and does not execute SQL.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove only objects created for this lesson from the disposable schema/session, or restore the lab snapshot. Never run reset or destructive commands against production.

content_blocks.title: Version, security, and safety note
content_blocks.text: Use MySQL 9.7 LTS documentation as the default stable-track reference; verify behavior against MySQL 26.7 documentation when relevant and label any MySQL 8.4-specific fact. Examples are static references, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run mutation, privilege, replication, backup, and recovery examples only in an isolated lab.

content.task: Try it yourself: Capture an execution plan, record the starting query and result, change one index or query decision, and compare measurements. Submit the query, result or decision record, plus one edge case and one verification step.
task_acceptance_criteria: Address the core behavior in performance and load testing using a MySQL-specific example or a clear operational plan.
State the expected result and demonstrate how it would be verified in the selected environment.
Identify one relevant edge case, permissions boundary, operational risk, or version assumption.
hints: Start by identifying the question that performance and load testing needs to answer.
Reduce the example to the smallest meaningful row set or operational change, then write down the result you expect.
Check the applicable official manual and version note before treating the reference output as guaranteed.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a sample result proves the whole design is correct.
common_mistakes.why: Edge cases such as NULLs, duplicate matches, concurrency, privileges, or version differences may change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a targeted boundary case and record the server version, schema and expected result.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a mutating or administrative example in the wrong environment.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data changes, access grants, and recovery commands may have persistent impact.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable lab, preview targets and permissions, and write a reset/recovery plan before executing.

summary: An application connection is a trust boundary. Keep credentials outside source control, use parameterized queries for values, define transaction boundaries, and handle lost connections without assuming a request was never committed.
